title: Projected Neural Additive Models as Universal Approximators
claim: Linearly projecting inputs, applying independent single-variable nonlinear functions, and linearly recombining gives an expressive yet interpretable additive model.
layout: Single panel, left-to-right network graph, with matrix equations beneath the linear stages
description: A neural network diagram flowing left to right. On the left, four blue input nodes (chi) connect through red dashed lines, labeled 'Linear', to six purple projected nodes (z). Each z node feeds its own green rounded box containing a small MLP, labeled 'Nonlinear, f_i := MLP_i'. The outputs of the MLPs (olive nodes) connect through blue dashed lines, labeled 'Linear', to a single light-blue output node y-hat. A black arrow from a noise node epsilon also points to y-hat. Under the left stage, a heatmap matrix T times a vector chi equals z, with the equation 'Tχ = z'. Under the right stage, a heatmap row vector times a green column vector equals a scalar, with the equation 'Σ ζ_i f_i(z_i) + ε = ŷ'. The eye goes first to the dense red crossing arrows and the stacked green boxes.
caption: Architecture of the PNAM. The output by is predicted via a linear combination of single-variable functions, parameterized by independent MLPs, which are evaluated on linear combinations of the inputs χ. The transformation T and weighting coefficients ζ (both denoted with dashed lines) can be optimized to yield sparser (and more interpretable) solutions.
abstract: Neural additive models (NAMs) offer interpretability but lack expressivity due to their rigid additive structure, whereas multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) achieve universal approximation at the cost of transparency. We establish the first theoretical foundation for projected neural additive models (PNAMs), which augment NAMs with a learnable linear transformation $\boldsymbol{T}$ to capture cross-variable interactions. While standard NAMs cannot approximate even the simplest interaction term $Ï_1 Ï_2$ because their cross-derivatives are identically zero, we prove that PNAMs are universal approximators and characterize the minimum number of projections required for exact polynomial representation. Furthermore, we derive an approximation rate of $\mathcal{O}(M^{-s / (N - 1)})$ for $\mathcal{C}^s$ functions (i.e., functions with $s$ continuous derivatives), where $M$ denotes the number of projections and $N$ the input dimension; this rate is known to be optimal for ridge function approximation. To recover interpretability from the projected inputs, we introduce structured sparsity regularizers and post-hoc symbolic regression techniques that enable global input ranking, parameter pruning, and the conversion of learned bases into compact analytical expressions. Experiments on knot theory invariants, MNIST, and phase field fracture mechanics demonstrate that PNAMs match or surpass similar architectures in accuracy while discovering salient features and yielding symbolic models with orders of magnitude fewer parameters.
